rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - cross-sectional household survey of 383 farmers (195 MI, 187 control) in four Tanzanian districts, Feb-Mar 2021, with gross margin, partial budgeting and regression analysis. Q2: Sections 3.2.2-3.2.5, Table 3, Figures 3-8 - MI (drip kit) farmers had higher yields, revenue and gross margins than control farmers for nearly all vegetables in Hai, Kasulu and Kilosa; Section 3.3 - half of interviewed MI farmers used extra income for school expenses; Section 3.6 - 60% reinvested in more kits; Section 3.7/Conclusions - MI increased income and improved livelihoods. Q4: Figures 3-8 and Section 3.2 - the study measures per-bed yield, sale price, variable cost, revenue and gross margin as the pathway from the drip kit to household income/livelihood. Q5: Tables 1, 3, 8, Appendix Tables A1-A4 - results reported separately for Babati (Manyara), Hai (Kilimanjaro), Kasulu (Kigoma) and Kilosa (Morogoro) districts and for several vegetable crops. Q6: Sections 2.1 and 3.2-3.3 - effects reported at household/farm level aggregated across districts (383 households in four districts), not a single plot. Q7: Section 3.2.4 and Conclusions - authors state from their findings that a higher per-unit price/market linkage is vital for the gross margin gain, that MI for income generation is more effective when combined with market-link initiatives, and that continued high yields are not guaranteed without soil nutrient analysis. Q8: Section 4 Limitations and 3.4 - cross-sectional snapshot design, no baseline data, possible spillover to control farmers, short (~12 month) participation. Q9: Figures 3-8 - standard error of the mean shown as error bars for yield, price, revenue, TVC and GM; Tables 4-8 report means with SD for poverty/food security indicators.
rows.notes: The row's function is labelled social_cohesion but the passage claims enhanced livelihoods; rated on the livelihoods claim. Own evidence supports higher income/gross margins and farmer-reported benefits, but multivariate analysis found no significant association between MI participation and poverty, food security or asset indices overall, with mixed district results (negative in Kasulu). The 'kit' bundles drip equipment with seeds, fertilizer, pesticide and technical advice, so the effect is of the package rather than drip alone. Q3 set to no: the quantitative survey and qualitative interviews are both farmer self-report and the interviews are only sparsely reported, so I did not count them as two independent methods confirming the same result.

notes: Full text available; some PDF layout duplication of text in Sections 2.2 and 3.2 but content is complete.
